P1.evidence: Setter notes were read back, which is the only call in this batch where that happens: 'I went through everything that you told to my friend, Kaila. Yeah. there's a lot going on over there, to be honest.' The frame was the usual truncated version — 'I just want to understand where you're at right now and how we can actually potentially help you with... If there's an alignment... if not, that's totally fine too' — with no 'what's in the way' or 'what you need'. No agreement was requested; the rep moved straight on. Open question ran well and in the prospect's own terms: 'brief me in your own words, like, what you're actually looking for.'

P2.evidence: Injuries were the one thoroughly run check — 'Any serious things?' then 'Anything else that I need to know of?' — which surfaced bilateral labral tears, the stem cell treatment, the metal bar and eight screws, and the flat feet, and the rep later probed the shoulders specifically ('because you mentioned those shoulder injuries, do you have like stiffness in them?'). Beyond injuries the baseline barely ran. Age, height and weight were never asked at all. Occupation was never asked — the rep learned only that the prospect travels constantly and has back-to-back meetings. Sleep and energy were never raised. The training week was described but never asked for as a week, and results emerged from a different question ('What's the biggest piece missing for you right now in terms of training?'). Diet was asked properly and probed on the travel failure mode.

P3.evidence: Only the surface layer ran: 'if you would have to say like, would it be like getting stronger or like overall mobility type of thing?' and 'Do you have, like, a specific goal with it that you want to achieve?' Nothing below it. The bridge question, the 'what does that do for you', the 'who else does that impact' and the drive through to identity or longevity were all absent — this call never left the gym. Two partial reflect-backs were offered ('So basically, you're looking for something that you could implement into your workouts when you're traveling, right?' and 'mobility would be the baseline for you and the foundation'), both about mechanics rather than motive. The rep noticed the prospect was atypical — 'you're not our typical client' — and treated that as a reason to skip depth rather than to find a different depth.

P4.evidence: Not run. No question about what he had tried, what happened or why it did not stick. The nearest approach was 'What's the biggest piece missing for you right now in terms of training that you do currently? Apart that you're bored with it' and a one-word 'Why is that?' after he admitted skipping leg day, which he answered with 'I don't enjoy it' and the rep accepted with 'Yeah, that's fair.' The prospect had handed over an obvious thread — he abandoned barre classes and running purely from boredom, which is the same pattern that will end a kettlebell programme — and nobody pulled it.

P5.evidence: Entirely absent. No two-year question, no settle test, no 'why not', no line in the sand. There is a defensible reason — a fit man with no complaint has a weak cost of inaction — but the script offers no alternative, and the consequence of skipping it showed up immediately: when hesitation arrived at the price there was nothing built to return to, so the rep discounted instead.

P6.evidence: The belief check was replaced with a temperature check: 'So how do you feel about overall?' and 'So does it sound like you want to do it, or like, eh?' The prospect's answer — 'Everything seems pretty straightforward' — is comprehension, not commitment, and he immediately asked for the price rather than giving one. The all-in question was never asked. The rep presented anyway without a clear yes, which is precisely what P6c forbids, and the objections that followed were exactly the ones a commitment check would have surfaced first.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and reached a soft agreement on the trial — 'Yeah, I think that would work' — but no payment was requested or collected, and the prospect left to 'check a few other things'. Because payment never happened, the Trevor onboarding booking, the agreement email and signature, and the welcome sequence were all unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: 'I'll think on it. I'll let you guys know' at 00:22:15. Exactly one scripted move ran — 'So what's coming up for you right now that's keeping you from actually moving forward?' — and it worked, producing a precise answer. The rep then dropped the play entirely: no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you there', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. Instead of continuing he cut the price, which converts a thinking objection into a discount negotiation.

Price was raised — 'for me to pay 6K to just get a program seems a little crazy for me' — so the trigger is present in form, but the prospect immediately disqualified money as the cause: 'it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid all the time.' No OC move ran: no isolation, no should-I-versus-how framing, no permission question, none of the six financial-picture questions. This is arguably correct — OC is the wrong play when capacity is not the blocker — but what ran instead was a unilateral price cut, which is worse than running nothing.

Script gap, and the prospect named it himself: 'what I want is not necessarily something that you guys normally sell. Like, I just want to buy a program.' He wants programming without the coaching relationship, and had said so at 00:07:55 before any pitch — 'it's probably less of a one-on-one coaching... and more so, like, just getting a program, working on it, like, using you guys as a resource when I need to.' There is no play for a prospect who wants a subset of the offer. The rep argued need ('you mentioned that you don't have, like, experience in caribals and, like, in complex movements') and the prospect conceded only month one, which is what led directly to the invented 30-day product.

Second script gap, and this one was a missed opportunity rather than a genuine dead end. The prospect anchored against his own in-person trainer spend — '1,500, 2K a month sometimes on trainers... to spend the same amount for virtual seems a little crazy' — but $6,000 over six months is $1,000 a month, materially less than what he already pays. The anchor objectively supports the price and was presented as if it undercut it. Nobody did the arithmetic out loud, and there is no scripted move that would have prompted it.

notes: Injury screening and the setter read-back were good; everything between them and the price was skipped, so the offer landed on a prospect with no established why, no root cause and no commitment. The critical failure is what happened under hesitation: the rep answered a product-shape objection with three successive price cuts, ending at a quarter of the opening number, against a prospect who had explicitly said price was not the issue. Coaching point in one line — when the objection is scope, discounting it teaches the prospect the price was never real.
